Judicial Branch testimony in favor of LD 1965,Resolve, to Establish a Task
Force to Create a Court Navigation Program Plan:
Senator Camey, Representative Kuhn, members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Judiciary, my name is Julie Finn and I represent the Judicial Branch. I would like to provide
some testimony in favor of this bill.
LD 1965 creates a Task Force that would study the addition of court navigators to
provide guidance and infonnation about court processes and procedures to persons involved with the court system. In addition, they would be trained to refer court users to community-based resources and services depending on their needs.
The Judicial Branch is currently piloting a project at the York Judicial Center in Biddeford to provide volunteer greeters to the public. The York County clerk described the pilot
as follows.
"The York Judicial Center opened in 2023 and is a beautiful modern courthouse, but it's also big and can be intimidating for people who have never visited it. In
this pilot program We hope to attract volunteers who are comfortable interacting with the public and who are enthusiastic about helping people get the information
and resources they need quickly and with a minimum of stress."
The task force described in this resolve would assist court users with finding appropriate services after they leave the courthouse and would dovetail nicely with the Judicial Branch pilot
project already begim.
Members of the Judicial Branch staff would be happy to participate in the task force and assist in any Way that is needed and helpful.
Thank you for your time.

force, bringing together a diverse coalition of experts, including representatives from the University of Maine System, Pine Tree Legal Assistance, Disability Rights Maine, the National Alliance on Mental
Illness Maine, 211 Maine, the Department of Health and Human Services, and others. This group will
be tasked with examining similar programs from across the country, assessing the specific challenges faced by Maine's unrepresented litigants, and recommending a model that fits our state's courts and communities.

representative of the Judicial Branch, both of whom expressed support for this task force. In fact, a pilot
program was recently launched in York County that can serve as a model to be further explored.1
The goal is straightforward but significant: to develop a program that not only provides guidance on court processes and procedures but also connects individuals to essential cormnunity-based resources,

Overview of Court Navigator Programs
ill
Court Navigator--Buncombe County, North Carolma
In Buncombe County, North Carolina, a single court navigator offers services to anyone coming into the Buncombe County Courthouse. The
navigator is employed by Goodwill Industries International lnc., but works in the courthouse full-time. He has a deskjust past the main courthouse entrance and provides most services in the lobby. Services include answering questions, providing directions to get around the courthouse, and connecting people to resources available in the courthouse and in the community. In general, the navigators interactions with people
are brief. He does not collect information or engage in any follow-ups. For these reasons, the Buncombe County court navigator represents a light-engagement, single-navigator model of court navigation.
Court Clinician--Chesterfield County, Virginia
In Chesterfield County, Virginia, a single court clinician offers services
to anyone coming into the Chesterfield General District Court, with a focus on those with mental health needs. The clinician is employed by Chesterfield Behavioral Health but works in the courthouse full--time.
He has an office near the court entrance in the same hallway as the
General District courtrooms. The clinician answers people's questions
and addresses concerns they may have about the court process. He also meets with people to help them comply with court-ordered treatment, connects them to behavioral health providers in the community, and
provides direct therapeutic interventions himself, as he is a Licensed
Professional Counselor. The frequency of interactions with people
varies. He may meet with a person once or repeatedly over several
weeks or months. The clinician also collaborates with court actors by conducting mental health evaluations or consulting on behavioral health factors relevant to a case. In this way, the Chesterfield County court clinician represents a heavy-engagement, single-navigator model of court navigation that emphasizes mental health needs and
collaboration with court actors.

Criminal Justice Liaisons--Tennessee
In Tennessee, 34 criminal justice liaisons provide services in all 95 counties across the state. The liaisons work in criminal, municipal, county, and circuit courthouses and in county jails. Generally, each Liaison is assigned to a few counties. They provide services for anyone involved in the legal system, focusing on those with mental health needs. Employed by behavioral health agencies, the liaisons travel between courthouses,jails, and community locations throughout the week rather than being stationed in one place. Liaisons meet with people to discuss their needs and connect them with behavioral health, housing, and social service-related resources in the community. The liaisons frequently engage with people incarcerated in jail to assist in developing a release plan that includes connection to treatment and supports successful integration into the community. Liaisons typically
meet with a person just one time, though they may meet repeatedly over several weeks or months when necessary to ensure connection to services. The liaisons may also collaborate withjail and court actors by providing them with information on the status of a person's treatment
receipt. In this way, the Tennessee criminal justice liaisons represent a
moderate-engagement, single-navigator model of court navigation
that emphasizes mental health needs and jail release planning.

Criminal Justice Liaisons--Tennessee
ln Tennessee, 34 criminal justice liaisons provide services in all 95 counties across the state. The liaisons work in criminal, municipal, county, and circuit courthouses and in county jails. Generally, each Liaison is assigned to a few counties. They provide services for anyone involved in the legal system, focusing on those with mental health needs. Employed by behavioral health agencies, the liaisons travel between courthouses,jails, and community locations throughout the week rather than being stationed in one place. Liaisons meet with people to discuss their needs and connect them with behavioral health, housing, and social service-related resources in the community. The liaisons frequently engage with people incarcerated in jail to assist in developing a release plan that includes connection to treatment and supports successful integration into the community. DATE: TO: FROM: RE:

 May 19, 2025  Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary   Sam Warren, UMS Chief External & Governmental Affairs Officer  LD 1965, Resolve, to Establish a Task Force to Create a Court Navigation
Program Plan

Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary: I apologize that a Board of Trustees meeting at the University of Maine at Presque Isle prevents me from joining you in person today. I write on behalf of the University of Maine System, which includes the University of Maine School of Law (Maine Law), to convey our willingness to convene the task force that would be established by the bipartisan LD 1965, Resolve, to Establish a Task Force to Create a Court Navigation Program Plan.
With the state's only and public law school and as Maine's leading provider of behavioral health professionals, our System is well-positioned to lead this important work to develop a court navigation program plan. While we recognize the work detailed in the bill is significant, consistent with our public service commitment, our System is prepared to undertake this accelerated planning process within existing resources and looks forward to collaborating with the organizations detailed in Sec. 1.
While you heard from President/Dean Leigh Saufley in January, this is the first legislation focused on our law school to come to the Judiciary Committee this session, and I would like to use this opportunity to share an update about Maine Law with you.
As some members of this Committee will remember, Maine Law was on the verge of closure just five years ago, potentially making our state one of just two in the nation without a law school. System and State leaders agreed they could not let that happen and have made significant structural changes and investments in the intervening years to create a vibrant law school for all of Maine.
This past fall, Maine Law welcomed its largest incoming class since at least 2008 and with 270 total students, we are currently enjoying our highest enrollment in more than a decade. About half of the school's students come from outside of Maine, yet the overwhelming majority will stay in the state to practice after graduation. Their debt load is the lowest of their New England peers, and their first-time bar passage rate is now 89%, the highest among New England peers. Applications to join Maine Law this coming fall are up 60% over last year.

Testimony before the 132nd Maine Legislature.
Judiciary Committee
Testimony in favor of LD 1965: Resolve, to Establish a Task Force to Create a Court Navigation Program Plan
Chairpersons Senator Carney and Representative Kuhn, and Members of the Committee, my name is Suzanne Rudalevige and I live in Cape Elizabeth.
I want to say, up front, that my vision of making our Criminal Justice System more effective is to change our perspective from one focused on punishment to one which espouses a future oriented plan in which healing for both victim and violator is addressed in a holistic manner. This is the philosophy of Restorative Justice: helping the victim to come to terms with what has occurred and heal as much as possible from the damage done; encouraging the one who has done the harm to true accountability for his/her actions with appropriate restitution in whatever form; and including the community in finding this path forward.
I am much impressed with the restorative justice work of Danielle Sered at Common Justice in Brooklyn , NY, and highly recommend her book "Until We Reckon."
However, I definitely agree that providing the named support services ---- if actually delivered-- would promote the safety of the community and help those embroiled in the criminal system to find their footing to a more productive life.
I have recently been learning about the work of the Criminal Justice Taskforce, headed up by Deborah Ramirez, at Northeastern University School of Law"s Center for Law, Equity and Race (CLEAR).
Massachusetts now has 18 Community Justice Support Centers throughout MA , funded by the Commonwealth, which can be accessed by anyone in the criminal system, whether in or out of prison/jail. This is a viable model for us in Maine to provide court navigation. There is also emphasis on training judges in restorative justice so that, with those judges, there can be a well-founded understanding of appropriate alternative options beyond the "usual" system --- i.e. looking for remedies , rather than punishment.
The whole project remains part of the traditional court system but offers more diversion possibilities. This could conceivably have a beneficial effect on the willingness of defense attorneys to serve, or even reduce the number of attorneys required for criminal cases.
I am happy to supply information about the MA undertaking, if requested.
Thank you.
